extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of moral and political philosophy; statesmen, teachers, and general readers seeking practical guidance on manners, habit-formation, and civil conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and prescriptive guidance about moral/philosophical knowledge, cultivation of the mind, habit-formation, and civil (conversation/negotiation/government) arts, intended to shape behavior and policy. Emphasizes methods, cautions, and aphoristic rules for private and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize observations into precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations about temperaments, characters, and ordinary experience (e.g., 'lovers of quiet, lovers of action', 'sensitive, dry, formal, real, humorous') are frequently collected in words but not reduced to usable precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform scattered observations (from history, poetry, daily experience) into practical 'receipts' or rules for life rather than leaving them as loose descriptions: 'no man bringeth them to the confectionary that receipts might be made of them for use of life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inherent and external dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral philosophy should incorporate the influences of sex, age, region, health, beauty/deformity (inherent) and of external fortune such as sovereignty, nobility, birth, riches, want, magistracy, prosperity/adversity, and sudden rises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat diversity of grounds and moulds as essential knowledge similar to agriculture or medicine: different remedies/suggestions are required for different constitutions and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the affections as diseases and cures of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal subject of moral practice is the affections (passions) — their perturbations and distempers — and, therefore, one must know the characters of men, then the diseases (affections), and lastly the cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use history and poetry to study how affections are kindled, pacified, contained, disclosed, and how they interact; employ opposing affections (e.g., fear vs hope) as instruments of civil governance ('that excellent use of præmium and pæna').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counter-affection method in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil matters, set one affection against another to master or restrain a dominant passion (analogous to hunting 'beast with beast').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rewards and punishments to harness predominant affections (fear and hope) for social order and to bridle factions; use psychological counterbalances in policy and moral guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ controllable means to shape mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom, exercise, habit, education, example, imitation, emulation, company, friends, praise, reproof, exhortation, fame, laws, books, studies are all means within our command to affect will and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose regimens from these elements to recover or preserve the health of the mind; select and apply a subset suited to the person and situation rather than using one-size-fits-all remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid setting habit formation too high or too low
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming habits, beware of taking either too high a strain or too weak a strain at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too high a strain discourages diffident natures and breeds false facility in confident natures; too weak a strain prevents achievement of great tasks. Choose an appropriate starting level to sustain progress and avoid disillusionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice at two contrasting times
rubrics_metrics.description: Practise chiefly at two several times: one when the mind is best disposed, the other when it is worst disposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the best times to gain large steps and the worst times to work through knots and strengthen resilience so that middle times become easier and more pleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train by acting toward the contrary extreme
rubrics_metrics.description: Bear ever towards the contrary extreme of that whereunto you are by nature inclined (compare to rowing against the stream).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct innate crookedness or excess by deliberately exercising the opposite tendencies to reshape disposition (e.g., bend a wand contrary to its natural crook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect action to avoid resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind is more amenable when that to which you pretend is not plainly the intention ('tanquam aliud agendo').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the mind hates necessity and constraint, achieve change by disguising intent or pursuing the object as if it were something else to reduce resistance and make transformation feel more voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware chance-governed habits (counterfeits of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits governed by chance commonly prove but an 'ape of Nature' and bring forth something lame and counterfeit rather than genuine nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that exercise and custom are conducted deliberately; random or accidental practices will not form true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about reading and the timing of studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Books and studies influence manners but must be used with caution: some kinds of works (e.g., poetry, policy) may increase temptations or corrupt young judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young men are not fit auditors of moral philosophy (per Aristotle); policy books can make immature readers think virtues are merely utility-based. Tailor reading to maturity and temper one’s intake to avoid pernicious effects ('poesy vinum dæmonum').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against doctrines that make men overly precise or arrogant
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain doctrines of morality themselves may make men too precise, arrogant, or incompatible (Cicero on Cato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critical of moral teachings that substitute pedantry for natural virtue; check whether rules are coming from nature or merely a teacher's imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix good dispositions by vows and observances
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix and cherish the good hours of the mind use vows/constant resolutions and observances/exercises which keep the mind in continual obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured commitments and repeated practices to sustain virtue over time; this method is akin to religious discipline and effective for maintaining moral state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obliterate past evils by expiation and new resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove past faults practise some redemption or expiation, and make an inception or account 'de novo' for the time to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine penitential acts with renewed commitments to change; this twofold method helps clear old habits and enable fresh starts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and pursue reasonable virtuous ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Elect and propound to yourself good and virtuous ends of life that are reasonably attainable, and be resolute, constant, and true unto them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a man sets honest ends and steadfastly pursues them, he will 'mould himself into all virtue at once' — ends-oriented dedication produces broad moral formation more effectively than piecemeal habit practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity/unifying love as moral perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity (love) is the bond of perfection because it comprehends and fastens all virtues together and admits no excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for benevolence and imitation of divine goodness: other excellences can be excessive, but charity elevates and composes the mind without leading to vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for soundness, beauty, and strength of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The good of the mind tends to three qualities analogous to bodily goods: sound (without perturbation), beautiful (decent), and strong (able and agile for duties); these rarely meet together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize tradeoffs between inner tranquillity, carriage/decency, and robust capability; cultivate balance while allowing moderate pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain pleasure in moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind ought not to be reduced to stupidity; retain pleasure, confined in subject rather than vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow pleasures that are measured and appropriate to avoid deadness while preventing excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part division of civil knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil knowledge has three parts corresponding to society's summary actions: conversation (behaviour), negotiation (business), and government (statecraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate training and instruction according to these parts: conversation for social grace, negotiation for private/business counsel, and government for public policy; each requires distinct methods and materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation: govern countenance and speech; avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Urbanity in behaviour influences business and government; manage countenance and carriage so as not to destroy the force of words; retain dignity without intruding on other's liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being too curious about outward carriage (which wastes time) or too affected (which becomes a bad stage). Behaviour is like a garment — made to set off the mind, hide deformity, be in fashion but not restrict movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation/business knowledge should be practical and example-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom of negotiation/business has not been adequately written; the preferred form is discourse upon histories or examples (Machiavel's model), because example-grounded discourse best translates to particular actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer long-form historical examples or letters (e.g., Cicero ad Atticum) over abstract discourses; examples supply circumstances and constraints necessary to guide practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters and biographies for counsel; example-first writing
rubrics_metrics.description: For business and private actions, histories of lives and letters are more applicable than chronicles; example-first discourse (ground in full particulars) gives better guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching negotiation or business, present full particulars (circumstances) so the discourse is controlled and supplied by the example rather than vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish counsel from self-promotion and hubris
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a wisdom of counsel and a wisdom of pressing one’s own fortune; boasting that success is solely one's own is impolitic and unlucky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use maxims like 'Faber quisque fortunæ suæ' as spurs to industry but avoid public arrogance; attribute success to felicity as well as skill to avoid envy and misfortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provident stay of inquiry (avoid prying where harm may follow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commend the cautious restraint from investigating that which one would be loth to find; example: Pompey burned Sertorius' papers unperused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise discretion in inquiry; avoid opening investigations that will create more harm than benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not contend with fools
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise man finds no peace in contending with a foolish person—whether he becomes angry or laughs, he cannot escape entanglement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguments with lesser minds where the wise are disadvantaged and cannot 'quit himself well.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overindulge servants from youth
rubrics_metrics.description: If you nourish a servant delicately from childhood, later you will find him contumacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be measured in early favors to subordinates; excessive indulgence breeds ingratitude and insolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickness of despatch is a prime virtue for advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all virtues for rising to honour, quickness of despatch is the best; superiors often prefer readiness and diligence over excessive depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate promptness and timely execution as a key quality for reputation and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: On displeasure, do not withdraw
rubrics_metrics.description: When spurned or under displeasure, retiring is the unfit course; withdrawing leaves matters at their worst and robs you of means to improve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stand your ground and work to redress displeasure rather than retreating and ceding opportunities to make things better.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single exemplar of injustice undermines broader justice
rubrics_metrics.description: One public and exemplar iniquity disturbs the fountains of justice more than many private injuries passed by connivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect public examples of justice; avoid tolerating conspicuous corruption because it erodes public trust more severely than many lesser faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence or roughness can aggravate anger; temperate present answer pacifies
rubrics_metrics.description: A rough or silent response often intensifies anger, while a timely and temperate answer can break it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer present, calm replies to defuse anger; manage tone and timing to pacify disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procrastination multiplies impediments
rubrics_metrics.description: The path of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns: delaying preparation prepares many briars and impediments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid last-minute preparations; plan ahead to prevent accumulated obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions matter more than beginnings
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of an oration (or action) is better than the beginning; do not overvalue introductions at the expense of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus energy on achieving strong conclusions and results rather than only impressive starts or prefaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: First narrative holds disproportionate weight
rubrics_metrics.description: In a cause the first tale possesses much weight; the initial account creates a prejudice hard to remove unless falsehood is exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of first impressions in disputes and presentations; counteract misinformation early because first narratives persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-sounding simplicity outperforms artful flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial flattery that is set and studied does not penetrate deeply, whereas flattery that shows nature, liberty, and simplicity reaches deeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor sincerity and naturalness in persuasion rather than contrived, theatrical touch; simplicity resonates more profoundly with people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious reproving arrogant or scornful natures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproving an arrogant derisor often injures yourself; accusing an impious person may stain you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise care in reproving those prone to scorn; adapt the manner of correction to avoid self-harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give occasions to the wise
rubrics_metrics.description: If you give a wise person occasion, his wisdom will increase and be displayed; the practical wise require occasions to manifest their capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities for capable people to act; wisdom in habit shows more when put to use than when idle.

rubrics_metrics.name: The prudent perceive hidden hearts and adapt
rubrics_metrics.description: As faces shine in water, the hearts of men are manifest to the prudent; a wise person is fitted to many manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop perception and adaptability so you may apply appropriate counsel across diverse characters and customs.
